title: A single cloud decided to show up in my world builder
author: Oli4K
selftext:
My agent insisted that volumetric clouds would be too expensive and shouldn't be included in my Godot flight sim. It drew terrible solid clouds instead. They were so bad I didn't even want to take a screen grab. So I started a new, separate project in Codex instead of Cursor, model set Sol 6.1, just to experiment with volumetric clouds. Explained that the goal was to create a cloud system which would be owned by the sim, not a plugin. Then fed it a few papers on the subject of volumetric clouds and an hour later I could merge the files in the main project.

Clouds use seeded, connected lobes with procedural detail, a flat base, and controllable growth, drift, wind shear and dissipation. Lighting combines Beer–Lambert transmission, self-shadowing and an approximate multiple-scattering model. A GPU-generated 3D optical-depth cache avoids repeated shadow raymarches and blends between updates.

The simulator supplies cloud state and illumination through a small input API. The current prototype renders one cumulus. Multi-cloud scalability and further realism improvements are still the next step.

(Not sure which flair to add, hope I picked the right one)  
  
\# Procedural Cumulus Shape: Formulas



The current shape model combines eight connected ellipsoidal lobes using a smooth union, then adds procedural noise, erosion and a flat base. It produces a dimensionless density field for volumetric raymarching.



This is a controllable graphics model, not a fluid simulation. Its ellipsoidal distance functions approximate signed distance; the constants below are tuning values, not meteorological constants. Vector division is component-wise.



\## Smooth transitions



All smooth transitions use:



$$

S(a,b,x)=u\^2(3-2u),\\qquad

u=\\operatorname{clamp}\\left(\\frac{x-a}{b-a},0,1\\right).

$$



\## 1. Local coordinates, wind shear and growth



Let $\\mathbf{x}$ be the world-space sample position, $\\mathbf{b}$ the centre of the cloud base, $R$ the horizontal scale and $H$ the full vertical envelope height. World Y points upward.



$$

\\mathbf{p}=\\frac{\\mathbf{x}-\\mathbf{b}}{(R,H,R)}.

$$



Apply a prescribed horizontal displacement $\\mathbf{s}=(s\_x,s\_z)$ at the top of the envelope:



$$

\\mathbf{p}\_{xz}\\leftarrow\\mathbf{p}\_{xz}-\\frac{\\mathbf{s}}{R}p\_y.

$$



For development $g\\in\[0,1\]$, horizontal and vertical growth scales are:



$$

W=0.35+0.65\\sqrt{g},\\qquad V=0.16+0.84g,

$$



$$

\\mathbf{u}=\\frac{\\mathbf{p}}{(W,V,W)}.

$$



\## 2. Connected ellipsoidal lobes



The macro shape consists of a broad flattened base and seven overlapping shoulder/turret lobes. Their initial centres $\\mathbf{c}\_i\^0$ and radii $r\_i\^0$ receive small, reproducible seed-dependent perturbations.



Upper lobes activate progressively, for $i=1,\\ldots,7$:



$$

A\_i=S(0.08+0.035i,\\;0.50+0.035i,\\;g),

$$



$$

c\_{i,y}=0.12+(c\_{i,y}\^0-0.12)A\_i,

\\qquad r\_i=r\_i\^0(0.12+0.88A\_i).

$$



Their horizontal centres remain unchanged. The base lobe, $i=0$, does not use this activation rule. These lobe parameters are calculated on the CPU and supplied to both the rendering and light-cache shaders.



For each lobe, define its ellipsoid axes:



$$

\\mathbf{a}\_i=r\_i(1,\\lambda\_i,1),\\qquad

\\lambda\_i=\\begin{cases}

0.43 & i=0\\quad\\text{(flattened base)},\\\\

0.95 & i>0\\quad\\text{(shoulders and turrets)}.

\\end{cases}

$$



The approximate distance field is:



$$

d\_i(\\mathbf{u})=

r\_i\\left(\\left\\|\\frac{\\mathbf{u}-\\mathbf{c}\_i}{\\mathbf{a}\_i}\\right\\|-1\\right).

$$



Negative values indicate the interior. This expression has the desired ellipsoidal zero surface, but is not an exact Euclidean signed-distance function for an ellipsoid.



\## 3. Smooth union



Combine the lobe fields by repeatedly applying:



$$

h=\\frac{\\max(k-|a-b|,0)}{k},

$$



$$

\\operatorname{smin}(a,b)=\\min(a,b)-\\frac{k}{4}h\^2,

\\qquad k=0.09.

$$



The resulting field $D$ joins overlapping lobes without hard seams.



\## 4. Billowing, fine erosion and dissipation



Let $N(\\mathbf{q})$ be smooth, trilinearly interpolated 3D value noise in $\[0,1\]$, $\\boldsymbol{\\sigma}$ a fixed seed offset, and $\\boldsymbol{\\phi}$ a continuous detail phase:



$$

\\mathbf{q}=5\\mathbf{u}+\\boldsymbol{\\sigma}+0.25\\boldsymbol{\\phi}.

$$



Large-scale structure and fine detail are:



$$

n=0.65N(\\mathbf{q})+0.35N(2.03\\mathbf{q}),

\\qquad m=N(4.1\\mathbf{q}+\\boldsymbol{\\phi}).

$$



For billow strength $B$, erosion strength $E$, and dissipation $f$, all in $\[0,1\]$:



$$

F=D+0.16B(n-0.5)+0.10E(m-0.35)

\+f(0.10+0.15n).

$$



The first noise term perturbs the silhouette. The second adds finer erosion. Increasing dissipation erodes the body nonuniformly before it disappears.



\## 5. Final density



Convert the perturbed field into a soft volume mask:



$$

M=1-S(-0.08,0.04,F).

$$



A shared vertical profile flattens the underside and fades the envelope top:



$$

P=S(0,0.035,p\_y)\\,\[1-S(0.96,1,p\_y)\].

$$



The final dimensionless density is:



$$

\\boxed{\\rho=M\\,P\\,(0.65+0.35n)\\,

S(0,0.08,g)\\,(1-f)\^{1.3}}.

$$



Density is explicitly zero outside the supported envelope, when development is zero, or when dissipation reaches one. The implementation also rejects samples outside $0<p\_y<1$ or with $\\|\\mathbf{p}\_{xz}\\|>1.15$ after shear removal.



This density multiplies the extinction amplitude derived from liquid water content and effective droplet radius. It is not normalized to preserve a prescribed total water mass.



\## Example temporal controls



The optional laboratory animation prescribes, for age $t$ in seconds:



$$

g(t)=S(0,280,t),\\qquad f(t)=S(620,900,t),

$$



$$

\\boldsymbol{\\phi}(t)=(0.0006,-0.0025,0.0003)t,

\\qquad \\mathbf{b}(t)=\\mathbf{b}\_0+\\mathbf{v}t.

$$



It additionally uses $\\mathbf{s}(t)=(130,35)g(t)$ metres, $E(t)=0.18+0.57f(t)$ and $B=0.75$.



Sampling the same age and seed reproduces the same shape, independently of previous sampling history. The renderer has no lifecycle clock: the host supplies development, dissipation, phase, position and shear. The sim can replace the laboratory lifecycle entirely with values from its own atmospheric and thermal logic.



\## Temporal lighting



Slow morphology updates are rendered immediately, while optical-depth caches refresh at up to four updates per real second by default. Two GPU textures allow the old and new cached fields to blend smoothly. Large changes discard stale lighting. This is temporal light-cache blending, not screen-space temporal reconstruction or accumulation of stochastic samples.
